newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Consumer recovery boosts Kingfisher.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Consumer recovery boosts Kingfisher.

text.p: British retailer Kingfisher Plc on Wednesday said a housing market upturn and a revival of consumer confidence helped first half profits jump 47 percent and spurred recovery at its B&Q home decorating chain.

Kingfisher's shares leapt after it reported pretax profits of 109.6 million pounds ($170.4 million), up from 74.6 million in the first half last year. The shares were 11.5 pence higher at 676.5 pence by midday.
Chief executive Sir Geoffrey Mulcahy said all the group's businesses had done well, reflecting more buoyant trading but also that efforts to improve efficiency were paying off.
B&Q's turnaround was driven by improved market conditions, increased market share and a better operational performance.
At B&Q, the market leader in home improvement retailing in Britain, profits rose 48 percent to 47.0 million pounds from 31.8 million. Sales were up nearly 16 percent.
B&Q had been struggling in a depressed market, where overcapacity brought cut-throat competition from rivals like Sainsbury's Homebase and Texas Homecare and Boots Co Plc's Do It All.
But Mulcahy said the whole do-it-yourself (DIY) market grew by about four or five percent in the first six months of the year, against a flat market last year.
"B&Q we believe increased its market share in that six months," he told Reuters. He estimated B&Q's share of the DIY market rose by about 1.6 percentage points to 17.5 percent.
Mulcahy said the home decorating business had benefited from a revival in the housing market. "There's no doubt there is improved confidence in the general housing market."
But he warned against reading too much into revived consumer spending.

"I think that consumer confidence has definitely improved in the first half, but I would be relatively cautious about that because we've been through these times before and consumer confidence is somewhat fickle."

Mulcahy said the group was pleased with the performance at its electricals retailer Comet, which saw strong like-for-like sales growth of 11.9 percent and stable gross margins. It made a loss but this fell to three million pounds from 8.7 million a year ago.
The improvement came from better availability of merchandise in the stores as well as greater efficiency in running the business, the chief executive said.

Mulcahy was encouraged by a turnaround at Woolworths, which returned to profit of 4.6 million pounds, after a 900,000 loss last time. He said this was due to new product ranges particularly in kitchen and homewares and toys.
Superdrug, where profits rose by 9.3 percent to 16.4 million pounds, benefited from a switch to health and beauty.
French electricals retailer Darty was doing well in a tough French market. Profits were 42.5 million pounds, up from 40.0 million.
Mulcahy said costs throughout the business were under control, but there were some pressures from rental costs. ($1=.6430 Pound)
